This man became infamous after a Wheeling, West Virginia speech in which he claimed to have a list of 205 suspicious individuals in the State Department. Name this Wisconsin Senator who led a 1950's charge against Communists in the U.S. Government.

The actions of this colony's military were parodied in a work with the chapter "The Valiant Expedition of Captain Shrimp." One of its leaders wrote a section of the book Mourt's Relation. The military of this colony arrested Thomas Morton for his "Revels of New Canaan" involving an 80 foot Maypole. This colony's relations with the natives suffered after aggressive raids by military leader Myles Standish. Its governing document discusses their "voyage to plant the first colony in the Northern parts of Virginia," which was not where this colony was located. This colony was governed by William Bradford and was aided by the native Squanto. Name this colony founded by Pilgrims who had come over on the Mayflower.

This man's namesake "asparagus" refers to wooden poles meant to deter aerial invasion, while he dismissed the idea of an Atlantic Wall as "cloud cuckoo land." He rose to prominence after capturing a 10,000-man division retreating after Caporetto. Operation Bodyguard tried to mislead this man and his superior about a potential landfall at Calais, while Operation Crusader prevented this man's troops from succeeding in its siege of Tobruk. He was allowed to take poison rather than face trial after the failed July 20 plot of Claus von Stauffenberg. This man's forces lost to Bernard Montgomery at the battle of El Alamein in Egypt. Name this German leader of the Afrika Korps during World War II, a man known as "the Desert Fox."

In this city, Major Alexander Gordon Laing was reportedly killed shortly after arriving, while Rene Caillie won 10,000 francs for successfully returning from here. It receives commodities from the Taoudenni mines, while in the past, the arrival of salt from Teghaza was memorably described in the accounts of Leo Africanus. A library in this city is named for scholar Ahmed Baba, who was exiled after this city was conquered by Ahmad al-Mansur's Moroccan forces. It is home to the Djinguereber Mosque and the medieval center of learning at the University of Sankore, which were built during the reign of a king noted for his gold-laden pilgrimage to Mecca. Name this mythically wealthy African city in Mali, once home to a palace of Mansa Musa.

James Reston wrote that this work's speaker was "militant and sad." Clarence Jones suggested adding lines about defaulting on a "promissory note" that were incorporated into this text, whose speaker claimed that he had come to "cash a check" and refused to believe that the bank was bankrupt. This text was originally known as "Normalcy, Never Again" and incorporated phrases from an earlier speech given at Cobo Hall in Detroit at an event organized by Asa Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin. This speech said that people should be judged "not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character." This work ends by exclaiming that "Thank God Almighty we are free at last!" name this speech delivered by Martin Luther King on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

Before this event took place, Gaspar Fagel wrote letters denouncing the policies of one participant. Near its end, false rumors of an army revolt began in the "Irish night" hysteria. During this event, Patrick Sarsfield's forces were beaten at the battle of Reading. It was set in motion by a letter sent by nobles known as the Immortal Seven, and during it, favorable winds ensured a successful crossing for the ship Brill. The success of this event was cemented two years later by the Battle of the Boyne and a year later by the passing of the Bill of Rights. It featured a monarch from the House of Orange making a landing at Torbay and encountering generally little resistance. Name this 1688 event in which James II was replaced as English monarch by William and Mary.

This man's domestic life was fleshed out in letters he sent to his teacher while vacationing at Alsium. As a youth, he was tutored by the grammarian Fronto. This man's general Avidius Cassius captured the Parthian city of Ctesiphon, while his co-ruler died during the Antonine Plague. Married to Faustina the Younger, this man wrote a work that bears the note it was written "among the Quadi at the Granua." His co-emperor was Lucius Verus, who died while fighting with this man along the Danube River in the Marcomannic Wars. This man was succeeded by the mentally unstable gladiator aficionado Commodus. Name this Roman author of the Stoic text Meditations, the last of the "Five Good Emperors."

One prince of this dynasty was posthumously named "Emperor Yi," but was later demoted thanks to the actions of the "Jirgalang faction." The military of this dynasty carried out the Yangzhou massacre to punish resistance. Besides Princes Dorgon and Dodo, another military leader of this dynasty opposed the Wuchang Uprising and was named Yuan Shikai. It faced a rebellion led by a man claiming to be the brother of Jesus Christ, Hong Xiuquan, as well as an invasion by the Eight-Nation Alliance that resulted in the flight of Dowager Empress Cixi. This dynasty ended with the abdication of the child emperor Puyi and endured the Taiping and Boxer Rebellions, as well as losses in two Opium Wars. Name this final Chinese dynasty.

Four days before this event began, a rally featured such speakers as Markus Wolf and Marianne Birthler. It was arguably set in motion by a press conference that featured the ad-libbed words "effective immediately, without delay" in response to a question by Tom Brokaw. This event had been called for two years earlier in a speech described as "extreme" and "unpresidential" by Howard Baker. It was celebrated the following month by a Leonard Bernstein concert. This event began soon after the resignation of Erich Honecker and the ascension of Egon Krenz, and it had been famously commanded by Ronald Reagan in a challenge to Mikhail Gorbachev at the Brandenburg Gate. Name this event begun on November 9, 1989, which toppled a structure dividing a German city.

After a whipping incident, members of this group committed the Boyd massacre by killing over 60 sailors. One leader of this group cut down a pole to initiate the Flagstaff War, while members objected to a certain tax in the Dog Tax War. Their culture was documented in the writings of Sir George Grey, a governor-general. Members fought against each other in the battle of Te Ahuahu, and Europeans who joined them were called "Pakeha." This group was severely depleted in the Musket Wars, while they fought the British under the leadership of Hone Heke. When negotiating with William Hobson, they signed the Treaty of Waitangi. This people have designated seats in the Wellington Parliament. Name this native people of New Zealand.

In one speech before Congress, this man said he was not at the Battle of Stillman's Run, but did have a "good many bloody struggles with the mosquitoes." In another speech, he said "Let us have faith that right makes might." This man denounced "that attractive rainbow" of the war against Mexico and asked for proof of Mexican belligerence in the Spot Resolutions. He used a Farmers' Almanac showing the position of a moon while defending "Duff" Armstrong in a murder trial. This man gave the Cooper Union speech and also stated that "I believe this government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free" in his "House Divided" speech. Name this man who staged an 1858 series of debates with Stephen Douglas before winning the presidency two years later.

In 1987, graverobbers sawed off this deceased world leader's hands and held them for ransom. His return to his country was marred by the Ezeiza massacre, which killed members of the Montoneros. In 1951, this leader opened the Republic of the Children theme park, four years before being forced into exile. This man tried to cultivate European relations with the "Rainbow Tour." While imprisoned, his followers had earlier staged a 1945 protest at the Plaza de Mayo. This man's followers were known as the "shirtless ones" or descamisados. He was succeeded by his third wife Isabel, while his popular second wife was a former actress who died of cancer at age 33. Name this leader of Argentina who was married to the woman known as Evita.

One member of this group, Charlie Siringo, wrote the book Two Evil Isms comparing this group to anarchism. Another member, James McParland, used the alias "James McKenna" when working for Franklin B. Gowen. Dashiell Hammett worked for this group and used his experiences when writing about the Continental Op. The logo of this group was an open eye with the slogan "We never sleep." One member infiltrated the organization known as the Molly Maguires. Its namesake and founder foiled an assassination plot against Abraham Lincoln prior to being inaugurated, and members of this group were hired to track Jesse James and the Reno Gang. Name this detective agency founded in 1850, whose employees frequently worked as strikebreakers.

This country is the subject of John Dower's book Embracing Defeat. It hid artillery at an officer's club fake "swimming pool" in another nation as part of a scheme involving an explosion at a railway. This country paid a fine after sinking the gunboat Panay, and it was opposed by Claire Chennault's volunteer air force. Its navy staged a successful attack in the Battle of Port Arthur during a conflict ended by negotiations in Maine with a rival country's diplomat Sergei Witte. One of its monarchs announced this country's surrender in the Jewel Voice Broadcast. This country's forces won a war ended by the Treaty of Portsmouth and committed the Rape of Nanking in China. Name this country led by Hirohito during World War II.

This man's military defeated king Totila at the Battle of Taginae, and he employed the unpopular tax collector John the Cappadocian. He set up an "Eternal Peace" with Khosrau I that did not last twenty years. This ruler dispatched Mundus to massacre dissidents, who had chosen Hypatius to replace this man. His reign is covered in the Secret History of Procopius and he was married to the powerful Theodora. This ruler was forced to dismiss his adviser Tribonian after tension at the Hippodrome's chariot races turned into the Nika riots. During his reign, the Corpus Juris Civilis law code was compiled and his general Belisarius defeated the Vandals. Name this Byzantine emperor who ordered the building of the majestic Hagia Sophia.

One member of this dynasty was married to Gerberga, whose flight to a rival kingdom following his death prompted that kingdom's destruction. Another member was ridiculed for bribing the chieftain Rollo to end the siege of a major city. Another member of this dynasty had a hunchbacked son found guilty of treason and was temporarily married to the daughter of Desiderius. Two members would sign the Treaty of Mersen and also pledge the Oath of Strasbourg in opposition to their brother. After the death of Louis the Pious, members of this dynasty, such as Lothair and Charles the Bald, ended a civil war by signing the Treaty of Verdun. Name this dynasty whose most famous rulers were Pepin the Short and Charlemagne.

The Taylor Prism describes a ruler of this empire, who reportedly shut up an opposing king in his residence "like a bird in a cage." This empire built a capital at Dur Sharrukin and it defeated the Egyptians under Taharqa. It was while trying to help this empire that Pharaoh Necho fought Judah in the Battle of Megiddo. This empire effectively fell during a sacking of the capital by Medes and Chaldeans. One of its rulers had a namesake library at the capital where the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh was found. It conquered the Northern Kingdom of Israel, but could not take Jerusalem. Name this Mesopotamian empire with such rulers as Ashurbanipal, which fell during the sacking of its capital, Nineveh.

One important document in this event was the "Panizzardi telegram." During it, an assailant shot lawyer Fernand Labori in the back and Hubert-Joseph Henry slit his throat with a razor while in a prison cell. Georges Picquart's actions during this event resulted in him being reassigned to Tunisia. The public was stirred up in this event by the racist writings in the paper La Libre Parole. Much of the blame eventually went to Ferdinand Esterhazy. A letter about this scandal was addressed to Felix Faure, published by Georges Clemenceau in his newspaper L'Aurore, and was titled "J'accuse" by author Emile Zola. Name this French political scandal in which the namesake Jewish artillery officer was erroneously sent to Devil's Island.

This man married the daughter of the first Secretary of the Interior, Thomas Ewing. His wife, Ellen described how he suffered "melancholy insanity" after being put on leave by Henry Halleck. During the election of 1884, this man took himself out of the race by saying "I will not accept if nominated and will not serve if elected." He established what became the Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth. His namesake "neckties" were broken railroad rails that his men wrapped around tree trunks. During one campaign, this man said his men would "forage liberally on the country" and have the right to "destroy mills, houses, cotton-gins, etc." For 10 points name this Union Civil War general, who led a brutal "march to the sea" in Georgia.

This man dissed the Catholic church as an "Asian monarchy' in the pamphlet The Vatican Decrees in their Bearing on Civil Allegiance. During his ministry, the Cardwell Reforms abolished peacetime flogging and Lord Cavendish was stabbed to death by the "Invincibles." This man attacked an opposing ministry in speeches given during the "Midlothian Campaign," and denounced Ottoman atrocities in a pamphlet about "Bulgarian Horrors." He was Prime Minister when "Chinese" Gordon was killed by the Mahdi's forces at Khartoum, and he unsuccessfully introduced both the First and Second Irish Home Rule Bills in the 1890's. Name this man who served four separate terms as Prime Minister under Queen Victoria, a Liberal who feuded with Benjamin Disraeli.

One depiction of this conflict shows William Johnson sparing the life of the captured Baron Dieskau. Soldiers were dispatched to defend a structure by Robert Dinwiddie. During this conflict, atrocities committed near Lake George at Fort William Henry prompted the later harsh treatment of captives after a siege won by Jeffrey Amherst. One side in this conflict was dispatched to capture Fort Duquesne, but failed when Edward Braddock was killed at the Battle of the Monongahela. In one early engagement, soldiers hastily constructed Fort Necessity. During this conflict, James Wolfe and Louis Montcalm died at the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec. Name this American phase of the Seven Years' War, in which Britain took possession of Canada.

This work was first published on the so-called "Dunlap broadsides." In a painting depicting it, one figure is possibly stepping on the foot of his political rival. The success of this work was assured after one figure dramatically arrived after riding eighty miles through a storm; that man was Caesar Rodney. It was drafted by the Committee of Five, including Robert Livingston and Roger Sherman. This text begins by noting "in the course of human events," people may choose "to dissolve political bands." It features the line "We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men are created equal." name this document featuring a large John Hancock signature, which was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.

This ruler pushed through the appointment of Leo VIII as Pope and had to depose Benedict V to keep Leo as pontiff. He was opposed by revolts led by Conrad the Red and his half-brother Thankmar. This ruler expanded his territory by marrying Adelaide and becoming "King of the Lombards," and won one battle against the forces of Bulcsu, Lel, and Sur. He moved into Italy to fight his longtime foe, the usurper Berengar, and appointed his brother Bruno the Archbishop of Cologne. The son of Henry the Fowler, this man beat the Magyars at Lechfeld, and received his most famous title after saving the Papal States and Pope John XII. Name this Saxon crowned in February 962 as effectively the first Holy Roman Emperor.

In one battle fought in this modern day country, the winning side, after much deliberation, adopted the aggressive tactics of Major Eyre Coote. The surgeon John Zephaniah Holwell wrote a probably exaggerated account of atrocities here, while for his actions in this country, Warren Hastings was impeached for crimes and misdemeanors. A rebellion in this country was partly sparked by the fact that rifle cartridges were coated with tallow. Robert Clive won the Battle of Plassey here. One incident in this country took place at Fort William, with the accusation that 146 British prisoners were placed in a cramped prison, with only 23 surviving. Name this modern day country, the former home of the Black Hole of Calcutta.

The leader of this event took command after Pringle Stokes committed suicide. It was planned by Francis Beaufort and it involved use of a tool known as the Sympiesometer. During this event, the man known as "Jemmy Button" was returned to his people. Its most notable participant may have acquired Chagas disease during it and afterwards abandoned his plans to become a parson. This event included encounters with the savage Yaghan natives and the obtaining of remains of the rhea bird. Officially led by Robert FitzRoy, this event led one participant to reject Charles Lyell's geological theories and develop an interest in the birds of the Galapagos. Name this 1830's trip around the coast of South America in which Charles Darwin made lots of observations.
second voyage of the HMS Beagle

One story says this man punished his aide Mummius by inflicting decimation upon his defeated troops. He lost a battle to the numerically inferior forces of the Spahbod Serena, in which his "testudo formation" temporarily blocked horse archers but was useless in melee combat. The commander of the right wing at the Battle of the Colline Gate, he notoriously employed a fire-fighting brigade which put out fires after he acquired the homes. This man won the Battle of the Siler River to end the Third Servile War, after which he ordered the crucifixion of the followers of the ex-gladiator Spartacus. After losing to the Parthians at Carrhae, he reportedly had molten gold poured down his throat. Name this wealthy Roman who formed the first Triumvirate with Pompey and Caesar.

This conflict is depicted in the painting And When Did You Last See Your Father?, which shows a young boy being questioned. During one battle, the hunting poodle Boye, who was rumored to have magical powers, was killed, distressing his owner, Prince Rupert of the Rhine. Politicians were banned from holding military office in this conflict thanks to the Self-denying Ordinance. One figure formed a cavalry unit called "Ironsides." The winning side in this war conducted "Pride's Purge" to remove dissenters. Its first phase contained the battles of Marston Moor and Naseby, the latter featuring the New Model Army. Name this conflict between the Roundheads and Cavaliers, which resulted in the execution of Charles I and the formation of a government led by Oliver Cromwell.

In one speech, this man said that the "future is not one of ease or resting but of incessant striving." During his ministry, his country was invaded when opposing forces from the north crossed the McMahon Line in a conflict which resulted in the resignation of Defense Minister Menon. This man's military destroyed the Afonso de Albuquerque when seizing a Portuguese territory. He gave the "Tryst with Destiny" inaugural speech and during 1962, his country fought a brief war with China. This leader of the Congress Party officially became prime minister shortly after partitioning created a western neighbor led by Muhammad Jinnah. He was the father of future leader Indira Gandhi. Name this first prime minister of independent India.

This man led a commando action to capture the Duc de Villeroi during the battle of Cremona. In his later years, he led an unsuccessful relief campaign against the siege of Philippsburg during the War of Polish Succession. This man's first major victory prompted the signing of the Treaty of Karlowitz. He grew up in a French court, but after being rejected for military service by Louis XIV, he transferred his services to a rival empire, for whom he won the battle of Zenta and the 1717 siege of Belgrade against the Ottomans. During the war of Spanish Succession, this man teamed with the Duke of Marlborough to win the battle of Blenheim. Name this military commander for the Habsburgs, a nobleman from Savoy.

One figure from this state defeated John Coming Ball at the Battle of Black Mingo and had a loyal slave named Oscar. A so-called massacre was perpetrated in this state by Banastre Tarleton during the battle of Waxhaw, while one of this state's greatest heroes fought the British after his home was burned and was named Thomas Sumter. Key politicians from here included John Rutledge and the Pinckney family. During the Revolutionary War, the greatest mass surrender on the American side took place in this state when Benjamin Lincoln surrendered a city to Henry Clinton. This state was the site of Daniel Morgan's victory at Cowpens. Name this home state of the "Swamp Fox," Francis Marion, and the site of the devastating 1780 fall of Charleston.

This man's presidential campaign slogan was "I don't want to, but I've got no choice," and he was blamed for initiating the so-called "war at the top" when he opposed his former advisers for the presidency. This leader played himself in the political film Man of Iron and led discussion with the government at the Round Table Negotiations, which promised "semi-free" elections. He was arrested during the martial law imposed by his predecessor as president, General Jaruzelski. This man has credited his organization's success to the support of his countryman, Pope John Paul II. This former electrician co-founded a labor group after leading strikes at the Gdansk shipyards. Name this former president of Poland and leader of the trade union Solidarity.

Before taking the throne, this man's quarrel with chancellor William Longchamp was resolved by the Archbishop of Rouen. He was opposed by the "Army of God" led by Robert Fitzwalter. This king's opposition to the appointment of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury led to his excommunication by Innocent III. He failed to reclaim Normandy from France after his allies lost to Philip Augustus at the battle of Bouvines. This man made a power play while his brother was away on the Third Crusade and later faced opposition from barons who met with him at Runnymede to form an agreement limiting his power. Name this youngest brother of Richard I who was forced to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215.

In this conflict, the Taylor-Rostow report provided the basis for increased aid to one side. The Peers Commission investigated one incident during it. The term "shake 'n bake sergeants" referred to one side's forces in this war. One book about it focused on John Paul Vann, was written by Neil Sheehan, and was titled A Bright Shining Lie. A key bombing campaign in this war was code-named Operation Rolling Thunder. One country started fighting after a questionable attack on the Maddox and C. Turner Joy. During this conflict, American forces used a defoliating chemical known as Agent Orange. Name this Asian war which featured such events as the My Lai Massacre and the Tet Offensive.

One side in this battle employed the tactic of "hugging the enemy," where fighting from close range minimized the effectiveness of long-range firepower. Prior to this battle, one side's orders declared "Not a step back." In this battle, an apartment building was held for two months through an anti-tank rifle mounted on the roof at Pavlov's House. This battle featured an assault on the Romanian 3rd Army to allow the encirclement of the German 6th Army of General Paulus in Operation Uranus. This battle reversed the eastward momentum of Operation Barbarossa. Name this battle in which German forces were unable to capture and hold a Russian city on the Volga River.

This man called for justices to travel the land and issue writs of Quo Warranto to inquire into the legal rights of the lords through the Statute of Gloucester. Prior to his ascension to the throne, this man and Gilbert de Clare won the Battle of Evesham, ending the Second Barons' War. This king arranged a truce with Philip the Fair and returned to England following news of defeat at the Battle of Stirling Bridge. Upon his return, he organized an invasion that secured victory at Falkirk, where he defeated the forces of William Wallace. Identify this English king who succeeded Henry III and was known as "Hammer of the Scots."

This man secretly funded and helped organize the plaintiff's case in Giles v. Harris. In one speech, he mentioned the possibility of being "as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand" and instructed his audience to "cast down your bucket where you are." The Niagara Movement condemned this man's speech in Piedmont Park as the "Atlanta Compromise," and called this author of Up From Slavery the "Great Accommodator" because he was willing to allow whites to continue to dominate politics. Name this founder of the Tuskegee Institute and rival of W. E. B. Dubois.

Shortly after taking power, this ruler defeated the Shardana sea pirates, many of whom joined in this man's personal bodyguard. This man memorialized the conquest of Nubia in the walls of the Beit el-Wali temple complex. He secured food aid for the people with whom he signed the first recorded peace treaty in history, and he led troops for his father Seti I. He celebrated the Sed Festival to mark the 30th year of his 66-year reign and ordered great building projects like the tomb of his consort Nefertari and the temple complex of Abu Simbel. This pharaoh also fought Muwatallis and the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh. Name this New Kingdom pharaoh.

A site at Wairau Bar exemplifies this people's kainga settlement. The first groups of these people preyed upon the moa and Haast eagle, and they displaced their native kumara tubers with potatoes following European contact. Robert Fitzroy's installation of a certain structure induced these people to fight in a war that led to Korareka's burning, a conflict incited by Hone Heke. These participants in the Flagstaff and Musket Wars are divided into iwi led by chiefs called rangatira, and a group of them who migrated to the Chathams became the Moriori. These people signed the Treaty of Waitangi with William Hobson. Name these indigenous people of New Zealand.

During the Jemdet Nasr period, this civilization started the use of cylinder seals. In one of this civilization's cities, buildings featured painted clay cone mosaics, and the White Temple occupied a terrace there. It began with the settlement of Eridu, and the kings of its city-states were known as lugals, one of whom developed the first known law code in Lagash. This civilization was the first to farm year-round by employing irrigation canals, and its priesthood worshipped Anu and Inanna. This civilization's Uruk period witnessed the development of cuneiform script. Name this earliest known civilization that included the first urban centers at Ur and Akkad.

Monarchomachs were political theorists belonging to this group, and this group established a colony in Florida before being killed by Spanish soldiers. The Conspiracy of Amboise was developed by these people, who lost most political rights in the Peace of Ales. The dragonnades were soldiers sanctioned by the king to convert and repress members of this group. Henry of Guise carried out the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre against these people, while the Edict of Fointainebleau revoked tolerance granted to this group in the previous Edict of Nantes. Name this group consisting of French Protestants persecuted in the 16th and 17th centuries.

In 2008, Mike Craft claimed he was hired by the mafia to kill this leader in hopes of luring Fidel Castro to this leader's funeral. This politician helped expand his nation's welfare state and regional development programs under the "Just Society" program. He used the War Measures Act to hunt down suspected terrorists after the minister Pierre LaPorte was abducted by the FLQ during the October Crisis, and his passage of the 1982 Constitution Act did not prevent him from being ousted by his party two years later. Name this Liberal, a Quebecois who served as the Prime Minister of Canada for fourteen years between 1968 and 1984, succeeding Lester Pearson.

This president opposed an amendment that would have made Jesus "ruler among the nations" out of respect for Jews, whom he had earlier targeted with General Order No.11. This man's presidency, which saw the Virginius Affair, also saw Oakes Ames fraudulently offer stock in a company contracted to build the Transcontinental Railroad. Fisk and Gould tried to corner the gold market on Black Friday during the presidency of this man, whose re-election bid over Horace Greeley was successful despite the Credit Mobilier scandal. Name this president and Civil War hero who nicknamed "Unconditional Surrender" who was elected president in 1868.

This ruler exempted women with three or more children from laws requiring them to have a guardian and prevented unmarried men and women from receiving inheritances. This emperor spoke of his own daughter, whom he exiled to Pandateria, as a "disease of my flesh." He successfully put down the rebellion of Sextus Pompeius and reportedly cried out "Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!" after the Roman defeat at Teutoburg Forest. This father of Julia the Elder was part of the Second Triumvirate with Marc Antony, whose forces were defeated by this man's admiral Agrippa at Actium. Name this first Roman emperor and adopted son of Julius Caesar.

The newspaper Qanun advocated legal reform during this country's 1906 Constitutional Revolution. A Cossack commander who became leader of this country after a 1921 coup sparked controversy by violating the sanctuary of the Fatima al-Masumeh Shrine. By nationalizing a predecessor to British Petroleum, one leader of this country prompted the CIA to overthrow him in Operation Ajax. In this country, the White Revolution was overseen by a leader who gained power after Mohammed Mossadegh. That leader was forced to flee in a revolution that also saw 52 Americans taken hostage for 444 days. Name this country once run by Shahs and Ayatollahs.

The poet Octavian Goga led the anti-Semitic National Agrarian party in this country, and during the Legionnaires' Rebellion, Horia Sima rebelled against a leader of this country known as the "Red Dog." Several leaders in this country's history took the title Conducător, including one a man who was targeted by Operation Tidal Wave and faced rebellion by former supporters in the Iron Guard. Another leader of this country was opposed by a movement started in Timisoara and put forth the July Theses. That man was executed, along with his wife Elena, on December 25, 1989. Name this Eastern European country ruled by Ion Antonescu and Nicolae Ceausescu.
